newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Kaunda, father of free Zambia, seeks comeback.
newsitem.headline: Kaunda, father of free Zambia, seeks comeback.

text.p: Kenneth Kaunda is a veteran African statesman who led Zambia to independence, fell from grace as the Cold War ended and now is being thwarted in his bid for a comeback by the man who ousted him in 1991.

President Frederick Chiluba, from a younger generation of politicians, approved a change in the constitution that barred Kaunda, 72, from standing in Monday's presidential election because his Malawian parents were born abroad.

"How can they say Kaunda is a foreigner -- Kaunda, who fought for our independence?" said one supporter at a weekend rally to promote a poll boycott by the former president's United National Independence Party, UNIP.

Sensing global changes with the end of the Cold War and rising discontent at home as the economy imploded, Kaunda ceded to calls for multi-party elections and peacefully conceded to Chiluba, ending 27 years as the "Father of the Nation".
He retired after a defeat of humiliating proportions but changed his mind in 1995 and became UNIP leader again.
Kaunda formed the anti-colonial UNIP in 1958, won power in 1963 and oversaw the end of British rule the next year, the first country in the region to win independence.
Following African trends he declared a one-party state in 1974 but pursued "humanism", his unique personal blend of socialism, devout Christianity and traditional African values.

In foreign affairs, he was the doyen of a group of seven southern African "frontline" states that led the fight against South Africa's policy of racial separation, apartheid. A close friend of South African President Nelson Mandela, he let the African National Congress make a home in exile in Lusaka.
He also played a major role in Mozambique's independence in 1975, Zimbabwe's in 1979 and Namibia's in 1990.
But it was decades of mismanagement which almost ruined the country, and the reign of his secret police -- though benign by the standards of other African countries -- that undid him.
Doubling of the price of maize meal, the staple for the eight million people in landlocked Zambia, sparked a three-day riot in 1990 in which 27 people were killed.
Kaunda's prestige fell apart as pay packets shrank, prices soared and the copper-dependent economy got sicker and sank deeper into foreign debt which still plagues it.
Diplomats and political analysts say Kaunda, who wears safari-style suits, waves a white handkerchief and is balding, still retains much affection and respect despite his record.
Kenneth David Kaunda, KK as he is generally known, was born on April 28, 1924, the youngest of eight children of a Church of Scotland minister in the remote north of the country.
Known as "Bichizya" -- the unexpected one -- he worked as a teacher and a mine welfare officer and entered politics in 1949 as a founder of Northern Rhodesia's African National Congress.
An emotional man, he is unashamed to weep in public and has a unique speaking style in which he emphasises key thoughts by repeating whole sentences.
"He has been a force for moderation and peaceful change in Africa generally over the last few years. I hope that's what he will be remembered for," said a senior Western diplomat.
